Empirical Research Plan  
“Do the health benefits of extra care given to ‘very-low-birth-weight’ newborns (<1,500 g) exceed the costs?”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RD) with an RD-IV extension.

Rationale  
• The clinical guideline that newborns weighing <1,500 g are classified as “very low birth weight” (VLBW) generates a discontinuous jump in the intensity (and cost) of neonatal care.  
• Birth weight is continuous, measured in grams, and cannot be precisely manipulated by parents or physicians ex-ante.  
• Thus outcomes for infants just below vs. just above 1,500 g can be compared.  
• Because the guideline is not enforced perfectly, the treatment jump is incomplete; therefore we treat it as a fuzzy RD and, for cost–benefit, use the guideline indicator as an instrument for actual medical spending.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Running variable: birth_weight_g (in grams).  
Cutoff: 1,500 g.

Definitions  
• Instrument (Z) – “VLBW classification”: Z = 1 if birth_weight_g < 1,500, 0 otherwise.  
• Endogenous treatment (T) – Intensity of care.  Main measure: hospital charges (or, in CA & HCUP data, cost-to-charge–adjusted costs).  Ancillary measures: length of stay, ventilation indicator, number of procedures.  
• Outcome (Y) – Infant mortality within one year (main), plus 28-day and in-hospital mortality.

Groups  
• Treated group (local): infants with birth weights just below 1,500 g.  
• Control group (local): infants with birth weights just above 1,500 g.

Timing  
• Running variable fixed at birth; treatment occurs immediately after classification, so no staggered timing issues.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of the VLBW guideline, expected mortality and spending vary smoothly with birth weight at 1,500 g.  
  Plausibility: 1,500 g is a convention, not a biological break. Medical texts state no sudden change in physiology exactly at 1,500 g.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: Parents/doctors cannot induce birth weight to cross the threshold.  
  Plausibility: Weight at delivery is hard to predict to the gram; gestational age is largely set prior to observable weight.

A3. First-stage relevance: The guideline causes a discontinuous jump in average spending/treatment.  
  Plausibility: Documented hospital protocols and prior clinical studies show discrete increases in tests and NICU resources at 1,500 g.

A4. Monotonicity (for RD-IV): The guideline weakly increases care for every infant; nobody receives less care because of being below 1,500 g.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One infant’s classification does not affect another’s treatment/outcome within the local bandwidth.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Heaping / Measurement error in birth weight (e.g., clustering at multiples of 50 g).  
  Remedies:  
  • Inspect density (McCrary test); drop observations recorded at exactly 1,500 g or multiples of 50 g;  
  • Use bias-corrected local polynomial estimators that allow for measurement error;  
  • Show robustness to excluding 10-g “heaped” bins.

T2. Discontinuous covariates (gestational age, sex, race) at cutoff.  
  Remedies:  
  • Plot and regress each covariate on the running variable;  
  • Include flexible controls for gestational age and other covariates;  
  • Employ “local randomization” checks within ±30 g.

T3. Simultaneous policy changes or coding shifts coinciding with 1,500 g.  
  Remedies:  
  • Placebo tests at fake cutoffs (1,400 g, 1,600 g, …);  
  • Year-by-year RD estimates to verify stability;  
  • Hospital fixed effects and hospital-specific bandwidths.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----- 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast loading
library(rdrobust)       # RD estimation
library(fixest)         # fast iv + OLS
library(ggplot2)

# ----- 1. Load & merge data ---------------------------------------
# assume single stacked file birth_data.csv for illustration
dt <- fread("birth_data.csv")       # must contain: bw_g, death_1yr, charges, covariates

# ----- 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------
cutoff <- 1500
dt[, bw_c := bw_g - cutoff]                    # centered running var
dt[, Z := as.integer(bw_c < 0)]                # guideline indicator
dt[, mortality := as.integer(death_1yr == 1)]  # outcome
# (optional) drop exact heaping
dt <- dt[ bw_g %% 50 != 0 ]                    # robustness: drop 50-g multiples

# ----- 3. Reduced-form RD: effect on spending ---------------------
rd_spend <- rdrobust(y = dt$charges,
                     x = dt$bw_c,
                     c = 0,
                     p = 1,     # local linear
                     h = 250)   # 250-g bandwidth
summary(rd_spend)

# ----- 4. Reduced-form RD: effect on mortality --------------------
rd_mort <- rdrobust(y = dt$mortality,
                    x = dt$bw_c,
                    c = 0, p = 1, h = 250)
summary(rd_mort)

# ----- 5. RD-IV: Wald estimate (cost per life saved) --------------
# First stage (local data)
bw_win <- 250
local <- dt[ abs(bw_c) <= bw_win ]

iv_est <- feols(mortality ~ 1 | charges ~ Z + poly(bw_c,2), data = local,
                vcov = "HC1")
summary(iv_est)

# Cost per life saved (inverse of IV coefficient)
beta_iv  <- coef(iv_est)["fit_charges"]
cost_per_death_averted <- 1 / beta_iv
print(cost_per_death_averted)

# ----- 6. Robustness: alternative bandwidth -----------------------
for(h in c(100,150,200,300)){
  tmp <- rdrobust(y = dt$mortality, x = dt$bw_c, c = 0, p = 1, h = h)
  print(c(h, tmp$coef[1], tmp$se[1]))
}

# Plot covariate balance example: gestational age
ggplot(dt[abs(bw_c)<=300], aes(bw_c, gest_age))+
  geom_point(alpha=.2)+
  geom_smooth(method="loess")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty=2)
```
The code can be replicated separately for each state or cohort and combined via meta-analysis.

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Prior:  
• Spending/charges: Discrete increase of ≈ \$10,000–\$15,000 per infant just below 1,500 g.  
• Mortality: Decline of 1–2 deaths per 1,000 live births (0.1–0.2 pp).  
Implied cost per life saved: \$5–\$15 million (undiscounted). Given roughly 70 expected life-years for a surviving newborn, the cost per life-year is \$70k–\$200k—within the range many health economists consider acceptable.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RD)  
(1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
-------------------------------------------------
C1. No manipulation of running variable (density smooth) ………………… 1  
C2. Covariate continuity at cutoff ……………………………………………………… 1  
C3. Correct functional form / bandwidth choice ………………………………… 0.8  
C4. Single treatment changes at cutoff (no compound policies) …………… 0.9  
C5. Local SUTVA & monotonicity ………………………………………………………… 0.9  

Average score ≈ 0.92 → Research design appears highly credible but still requires careful implementation checks (especially heaping and bandwidth sensitivity).

-------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
